prime.problem: The median of two sorted arrays looks like it needs a merge: O(m + n). The source demands O(log min(m, n)). That's only possible if you never look at most of the items, and search for where to cut instead of for a value.
prime.fits: Second binary-search card. It reuses the first_true template from binary search on the answer, but the answer space is "how many items the left half takes from the shorter array". Divide and conquer later reads it as T(m/2) + 1.
expect: cut (i, j) with i + j = k
valid cut: A[i−1] ≤ B[j] and B[j−1] ≤ A[i]
prime.goal: Explain why fixing i fixes j, why one comparison per probe is enough, and trace the cut search to the median.

attend: Once you decide the left half takes i items from A, why is the number from B forced?
Why are the four boundary values the only items that decide whether a cut is valid?
The loop tests only A[i] ≥ B[j−1]. Why does the other crossing hold automatically at the first i where it's true?
Why search over the shorter array, and what does that do to the probe count?
What stands in for a missing neighbour when the cut is at an array's end?

must: The left half must hold exactly k = ⌊(m + n − 1)/2⌋ items → choosing i from A forces j = k − i from B → the search space is one integer i in [0, m] → binary search it

A cut is valid iff A[i−1] ≤ B[j] and B[j−1] ≤ A[i] → then every left item ≤ every right item, so the cut equals the merged array's cut → the median is next to it (min of the right side, or the mean of two for an even total)

A[i] ≥ B[j−1] is false for small i and true from some i on → monotone → first_true finds the smallest such i → at i − 1 it failed, which gives A[i−1] < B[j] → both crossings hold with one comparison per probe
elevated: Searching the shorter array bounds the range at m + 1 → ⌊log₂ w⌋ + 1 probes: 3 for m = 5 however long B is, 20 for m = n = 10⁶
reference: the source's bisect_left(range(m), True, key=…) one-liner and its & 1 ^ 1 precedence trap
binary search on the value (≈ 1,280 compares for 32-bit ints)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw A and B stacked with a vertical cut through each, label the four boundary values, write the two validity conditions and the formula for j, and add one sentence on why one comparison per probe suffices.
checklist: k items go left; i from A fixes j = k − i from B
valid when A[i−1] ≤ B[j] and B[j−1] ≤ A[i]
binary search i over the shorter array, O(log min(m, n))
the test A[i] ≥ B[j−1] is monotone in i
the smallest passing i also satisfies the other crossing
median: smallest right item (odd) or mean of the two smallest (even)

retrieve.q: Explain why the median of two sorted arrays can be found without merging them, in terms of what the cut encodes.
answer: a cut says how many of the smallest k items come from each array
if the four boundary values are ordered correctly, the left side is exactly the k smallest of the union
so you only need the right i, found by binary search, and the median sits at the cut

retrieve.q: Walk through probe 1 of the card's example (A = [1, 3, 8, 9, 15], B = [7, 11, 18, 19, 21, 25], range i ∈ [0, 5]): i, j, the four boundary values, the test, and the move.
answer: A[i] ≥ B[j−1]? 8 ≥ 18 fails: B gave too many to the left

retrieve.q: You have 20 sorted arrays and need the overall median. Does the cut trick generalise? What would you use instead, and at what cost?
answer: no: with two arrays one integer i fixes the cut; with 20 arrays there are 19 free choices
binary search on the value: guess x, count items ≤ x with a bisect per array, O(20 log n) per guess
or a heap merge up to the middle: O((N/2) log 20)

compare.q: Both cards run the same first_true loop. What is the answer space and the predicate in each, and what makes each predicate monotone?
answer: pair distance: d ∈ [0, max − min], ok = count(d) ≥ k; more room never removes pairs
median: i ∈ [0, m], ok = A[i] ≥ B[k−1−i]; as i grows A[i] rises and B[j−1] falls
same template, very different spaces: a value vs a split point

compare.q: A sliding-window median uses two heaps; this card uses a cut. What does each maintain, and why can't either do the other's job?
answer: two heaps maintain the lower and upper halves of a changing multiset, O(log w) per update
the cut exploits two static, already sorted arrays with no updates, O(log m) once
heaps can't answer from sorted arrays without inserting everything; the cut can't handle inserts and deletes

predict.q: A = [1, 2], B = [3, 4]. Predict the final cut (i, j) and the median, and say which boundary value is −∞.
predict.answer: k = (4 − 1) // 2 = 1. i = 1, j = 0: the left half is just A's 1. B gives nothing, so B[j−1] is −∞. The right side's two smallest are 2 and 3, so the median is 2.5.

apply.task: Trace the cut search for A = [2, 4], B = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Compute k, then for each probe write lo, hi, i, j, the four boundary values and the move. Finish with the median and check it against the merged array.
apply.done: k = 3; probe 1: i = 1, j = 2, 4 ≥ 3 → hi = 1; probe 2: i = 0, j = 3, 2 ≥ 5 fails → lo = 1; final cut i = 1, j = 2, median = min(4, 5) = 4. Merged: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9], middle item 4.
apply.hint: The search runs over A (shorter), so i ∈ [0, min(2, 3)] = [0, 2].

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the cut position, or which value became −∞?
Could you explain why the second crossing comes for free without drawing the arrays?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: i → j, or valid cut → median?
When would you just write sorted(a + b) instead?
What will you look for in the LIS card: a binary search over an array you build yourself?
